hints.junior: Arrow keys did nothing, Enter did nothing — users had to click the result, which defeats the entire point of Cmd+K.
hints.mid: A search box that filters but needs a mouse for everything else is slower than the menu it replaced, because it forces an input-mode switch mid-task.
hints.staff: This is a focus-management problem wearing a search-UX costume — filtering is the easy 20%, focus trap and restoration are the invisible 80%.

hints.junior: Try navigating each mode using only your keyboard — type, arrow, Enter, Escape, no mouse.
hints.mid: Broken filters on type but ignores arrow keys and Enter entirely. Fixed supports full keyboard navigation and traps focus while open.
hints.staff: Tab in the fixed mode and it stays inside the palette — close it and check where focus actually lands.

hints.junior: Arrow keys move a highlight, Enter activates it, Escape closes and returns focus — all three, no clicking required.
hints.mid: The input keeps real DOM focus the whole time; aria-activedescendant just points at the currently-highlighted option's id.
hints.staff: Skip the accessibility layer and you get two compounding bugs: a keyboard trap that lets Tab escape into the page behind it, and focus silently falling to body on close.

hints.junior: Fuzzy match should reset the highlight to the top result on every keystroke, or a fast typist can Enter a stale selection.
hints.mid: Virtualized result lists need highlight-tracking against the full filtered data, not just the currently-rendered DOM slice.
hints.staff: Verify with a screen reader on: aria-activedescendant announcements, role=dialog with aria-modal, and aria-expanded kept in sync on the trigger — all three are easy to skip if you only checked visually.

sections.junior: A team shipped a command-K palette that looked right, but the arrow keys did nothing and Enter did nothing — users had to click, which kind of defeats the whole point.
sections.mid: The entire value of a command palette is never touching the mouse, so a search box that only filters on type is actually slower than the menu it was meant to replace.
sections.staff: This turned out to be a focus-management problem dressed up as a search feature — the filtering was the easy part, focus handling was the part that got skipped.

sections.junior: A real command palette needs three things: arrow keys move a highlight, Enter picks whatever's highlighted, and Escape closes it and sends focus back where it came from.
sections.mid: The trick is the input keeps real focus the whole time — aria-activedescendant just points at whichever option is currently highlighted, so it looks like focus moved without actually moving it.
sections.staff: Skip that layer and you get two bugs at once — Tab can escape the palette into the page behind it, and closing it can silently drop focus to the body with no trace of where the user was.

sections.junior: Try each mode here using only your keyboard — type to filter, arrows to move, Enter to pick, Escape to close.
sections.mid: The broken version filters fine but ignores every other key. The fixed version handles all of it and keeps Tab trapped inside while it's open.
sections.staff: Tab around in the fixed mode and notice it never escapes the palette — then close it and check that focus actually lands back on the trigger.

sections.junior: If arrow keys, Enter, and Escape don't all work with no mouse involved, it's not a command palette yet, no matter what shortcut opens it.
sections.mid: Track the highlight with aria-activedescendant instead of moving real focus per keystroke, and trap Tab inside the palette the whole time it's open.
sections.staff: Every single exit path has to restore focus the same way — Escape, click-outside, picking a result, even a route change — or the happy path ends up being the one case that loses it.
